transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~68 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marco (Redwood Platform), Lena (Atlas CTO), Omar (Atlas ML), Sofia (Atlas Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Discussed long-context 128k+ strategies, chunking, kv cache pressure, attention optimization techniques and quantization tradeoffs; agreed to run benchmarks.

Topics: 128k+ long context, chunking/windowing, KV cache behavior, batching at scale, quantization, VPC/on-prem issues, latency/throughput tradeoffs

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: ok everyone thanks for joining, um today we want to dig into the 128k plus long context ask from AtlasData, specifically the perf and infra implications.
[00:12] Lena: yep thanks Alex, this is lena. we have a few real world streams where a single request can be 80k to 200k tokens after PDF+OCR, so chunking is a must.
[00:20] Priya: hi lena, priya here — SE on the runtime team. quick question to ground the convo: are those 200k sequences single-shot prompts or you're planning to do retrieval-augmented workflows with chunking?
[00:30] Omar: mostly RAG, but sometimes we do end-to-end generation over full docs for summary jobs. so sometimes it's full context processing.
[00:38] Marco: just to add, on our side the key constraints are latency SLOs (sub-second for small requests), but for long runs we can tolerate minutes, provided throughput is predictable.
[00:50] Alex: right. so two primary axes: how to represent the long context (single massive input vs streamed/chunked with KV cache) and how the runtime manages attention computation and memory.
[01:05] Lena: can you give examples of chunking strategies you support? like sliding window vs semantic chunking?
[01:12] Priya: sure. at a high level we see three common patterns: 1) fixed-size chunking with sliding window attention (overlap), 2) semantic chunking (doc-level split using embeddings + toprank), and 3) hierarchical chunking where you pre-encode long sections into embeddings and only materialize tokens for top hits. each has different kv cache pressure.
[01:36] Omar: when you say kv cache pressure, do you mean memory for past key/value states grows linearly with tokens? that was our impression.
[01:42] Priya: yes, exactly. with standard transformer causal attention the KV cache grows O(n) per token which can blow GPU memory for 128k. our runtime mitigations are: segmenting KV cache by chunk and dropping older segments when using sliding contexts, compressing KV states (lossy quantized caches), and using attention approximations that avoid full dense kv storage (e.g. chunked attention).
[02:05] Sofia: compression for KV states — is that quantization or algorithmic? what's the impact on quality?
[02:12] Priya: both. we do FP16/INT8 quantization for model weights and can also quantize KV cache to 8-bit or 4-bit using lightweight schemes. quality impact is workload-dependent; for retrieval-based summarization we saw minimal regressions at 8-bit KV, but for free-generation there's more sensitivity. we recommend targeted evals.
[02:34] Lena: can you run a benchmark showing delta in ROUGE/QA accuracy when KV is quantized?
[02:39] Priya: yes, that's in the action items. we'll run the 128k synthetic pass and then a small sample of real docs.
[02:45] Alex: let me interject on attention kernels: our runtime picks different kernel strategies depending on sequence length distribution. for medium sequences (<8k) we use optimized flash attention kernels; for 8k-64k we switch to chunked attention with local-global mixing; beyond that we default to hierarchical or windowed attention per customer workload.
[03:08] Omar: what is chunked attention? is that like Longformer local and global tokens?
[03:12] Priya: similar idea. chunked attention splits tokens into blocks and computes intra-block dense attention plus select cross-block attention for global tokens. it's cheaper than full N^2 at scale. some optimizations use overlapping windows and sparse patterns; others use compressed global representations.
[03:27] Marco: and importantly our scheduler can route long-context requests to specialized nodes that have more GPU memory and different kernel stacks—so you don't pay the latency tax on every call.
[03:36] Lena: that sounds good. on the infra side we are evaluating a 16xA100 rack for heavy jobs. what throughput can you get for a 128k job?
[03:45] Priya: it varies a lot by model size and quantization. ballpark: for a 30B model with INT8 and chunked attention on 16xA100 we can sustain ~1-2 tokens/sec aggregate for end-to-end long-pass generation (including retrieval overhead). if you're just doing pass-through summarization (few tokens output), throughput is higher because generation is short.
[04:08] Omar: 1-2 tokens/sec feels slow — how is latency for the initial response if we stream?
[04:13] Priya: initial response latency depends on how you chunk. using prefix caching we can provide early partial summaries as soon as the first few chunks are processed; full-context coherent generation needs either hierarchical recomposition or reranking.
[04:27] Alex: also note the batching story: with long contexts batching across requests is harder. our runtime does dynamic batching based on token profile and available KV memory; you can enable elastic batching to increase throughput at the cost of latency.
[04:40] Sofia: anything special on the networking/VPC side? if we run Private, do you need any special ports open to do the benchmarks?
[04:47] Marco: for Private we provide an on-prem runtime image and orchestrator; benchmarking requires SSH + S3 access for sample data and an ephemeral TLS endpoint for coordination. we can do air-gapped benchmarking if needed — then we'd exchange artifacts out-of-band.
[04:59] Lena: security is a must — we need SOC2 level controls, KMS integration and audit logs. does Redwood Private support HSM-backed KMS?
[05:08] Alex: yes, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping, and we can enable audit logging at the token level. we'll share the security pack.
[05:15] Omar: back on quantization — you mentioned int4 for KV. How stable is int4 for KV versus weights?
[05:20] Priya: int4 for weights is getting stable with per-channel quantization but KV int4 is trickier because activations vary more; we have experimental int4 cache modes with fallback heuristics. we often recommend INT8 for an initial pilot.
[05:34] Lena: what's the impact on accuracy for int8 KV cache, any numbers?
[05:38] Priya: rough numbers from internal tests: for retrieval summarization tasks, F1/QA drops <1.5% at 8-bit KV; for unconstrained generation the drop can be 2-5% depending on length and prompt sensitivity. we'll surface concrete validation for your dataset.
[05:56] Omar: what about attention approximations like Performer or linearized attention? any support?
[06:01] Priya: we support several approximation backends; linear attention works for certain models but often requires retraining or adapter layers; chunked/local+global patterns are more generally applicable without model changes.
[06:15] Marco: from an ops perspective, we also maintain an auto-eviction policy for KV segments to avoid OOMs: keep-N-recent-chunks or score-based eviction. you can control policies per-route.
[06:27] Sofia: if we evict KV segments, do we lose context fidelity? how do you recompute?
[06:33] Priya: eviction trades off context fidelity for memory. for RAG flows we can re-materialize segments from retrieved embeddings when needed. for pure autoregressive flows eviction is destructive — you would need to re-stream earlier tokens or rely on compressed summaries.
[06:49] Lena: what about using embeddings + chunk metadata to create a compact context representation instead of full tokens?
[06:55] Priya: that's the hierarchical approach — you compress large chunks into vectors and then only expand the top-k during generation. it's very effective for long-document QA, and reduces KV memory dramatically. quality depends on embedding recall.
[07:06] Omar: ok practical question: can we run an initial benchmark with our dataset slices (10k, 32k, 128k) on Redwood Dedicated or Private to compare?
[07:13] Alex: yes. action items capture that. specifically Priya will run synthetic runs on a 16xA100 sim, and we should schedule an on-prem Dedicated bench with your infra.
[07:23] Sofia: we need a config template to provision the nodes and docker images.
[07:27] Marco: I'll share the config repo and an example compose/k8s manifest. note for 128k runs you'll want bigger host memory and nvlink enabled if possible.
[07:36] Lena: any guidance on model choice? open models that already have long-context optimizations?
[07:40] Priya: models like LongLLaMA derivatives or models tuned for long contexts are helpful. but often runtime-level tricks are needed regardless. we recommend 30B-70B families to balance quality and memory. quantization profiles available per model in our catalog.
[07:58] Omar: about cost — how much more expensive is a 128k run compared to a 4k run?
[08:02] Alex: ballpark: compute grows superlinearly if you do full attention, but with chunking you can often get 5-10x higher cost than a 4k request depending on chain-of-thought length and retrieval. we'll give you a cost estimate in the spreadsheet.
[08:18] Priya: one more runtime detail: we maintain per-route SLOs and can fallback to shorter-context models or cached summaries if the node is saturated; that keeps frontend availability.
[08:29] Lena: good. timeline — we want a pilot in two weeks if possible.
[08:33] Alex: sounds doable pending infra provisioning. we'll aim to deliver benchmarks within 7 business days and a pilot schedule.
[08:40] Omar: any limitations we haven't discussed? tokenization quirks maybe?
[08:43] Priya: tokenization across OCR artifacts can blow up token counts; we recommend a preprocessing normalizer to dedupe whitespace and remove OCR artifacts to reduce unnecessary tokens. also chunk boundaries ideally align with sentence boundaries to avoid quality issues.
[08:58] Marco: and operational note: if you go Private on-prem, we'll supply monitoring hooks that emit KV pressure metrics, memory/latency per shard, and a profiling trace for attention kernels.
[09:10] Lena: perfect. let's recap next steps.
[09:13] Alex: recap: (1) Priya runs synthetic 10k/32k/128k benchmarks and real-sample tests (due 2026-03-09), (2) Marco shares config manifests and monitoring hooks (due 2026-03-06), (3) Atlas provides infra spec and sample data (Sofia, due 2026-03-05), (4) schedule 2-hour on-prem benchmark slot next week.
[09:37] Sofia: confirmed I'll get data and infra specs.
[09:40] Lena: thanks everyone. please include the perf spreadsheet and security pack in follow-up.
[09:44] Alex: will do; closing now.
[09:46] (call ends)
